did_you_know.text: Did you know? Moses’ blessings before his death echo Jacob’s blessings to his sons at the end of Genesis. In both passages, the tribes receive descriptions of their character and hints about their future.

Did you know? In the Masoretic tradition, אֵשׁדָּת is written as one word but read as אֵשׁ דָּת, meaning “fire of law” or “fiery teaching.” Sinai, Seir, and Paran are names of regions in the southern wilderness.

Did you know? The word מוֹרָשָׁה refers to an inheritance passed from one generation to the next, not merely to private property. The Torah is therefore presented as the shared heritage of the entire community of Jacob.

Did you know? The Urim and Thummim were connected with the high priest’s breastpiece and were used, according to the Bible, to seek divine decisions. Scripture does not explain exactly what they looked like or how they worked.

Did you know? Joseph is represented here by two tribes because his sons Ephraim and Manasseh received separate tribal territories. The word רְאֵם is usually understood as a powerful wild animal, not the unicorn of legend.

Did you know? According to the territory descriptions in Joshua, Zebulun and Issachar lived in the north, in Galilee and around the Jezreel Valley. The Sages later developed the idea of a partnership between Zebulun, active in the practical world, and Issachar, devoted to Torah study.

Did you know? The tribe of Dan first received territory in the central part of the land, but Judges tells how some Danites migrated north and captured Laish, which was later called Dan. This is why the tribe became associated with the far north.
Did you know? Asher’s territory lay in western Galilee, a region well suited to growing olive trees. In ancient times, olive oil was used for food, lighting, and anointing.
Did you know? Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel, and it appears only in the book of Deuteronomy. The name is usually connected with the Hebrew root y-sh-r, suggesting uprightness or integrity.

Did you know? At the end of the blessings, Moses moves from addressing individual tribes to addressing all Israel, ending the chapter with an image of one people. The phrase “Happy are you, Israel” is a solemn declaration of national well-being and divine help.
